text.p: It's very easy to get lost driving down the narrow, winding streets of New York City's Chinatown. But a slightly metallic female voice said, "turn left at the next corner," and there we were, at our destination, a restaurant at 20 Mott Street.

With a few clicks of the remote control, we told our car's on-board navigational computer where we wanted to go. But we didn't know how to get there. Given simple instructions to "go forward for seven-tenths of a mile" or "turn left in 500 feet," spoken by the computer's female voice, we were able to drive from here to there without getting lost. When we made an intentional wrong turn, the computer remapped our route and got us back on course.

The on-board navigational system we used was designed by Alpine Electronics of Torrance, Calif. The company has just started selling its Voice Guidance Navigational System in the United States, at a price of about $2,000. The system is available at selected automotive electronics retailers or general electronics retailers.

Up until now, only a select number of rental cars were equipped with on-board computerized navigational systems. The Alpine system is available for general consumer use and is being marketed to business travelers, emergency personnel and upscale customers who want up-to-the-minute technology in their cars.
The system, using a small computer screen that fits near a vehicle's radio or tape deck, tells the driver how to get from point A to point B by use of maps as well as verbal commands.

The system works with a series of CD-ROMs that contain maps of numerous metropolitan areas. By using a remote control, the driver can instruct the computer to find a specific address or intersection and map out the best routes.
The NVA-N751 A model, used in our test drive, contains a database that provides information on places a driver needs to go, such as to an ATM or gas station, or the shortest route to a specific site.
An Alpine executive suggested the Alpine NVA-N751A would be appropriate for fire, police or other emergency personnel who needed to get somewhere fast.
The NVA-N751 A has an auto-route search function, destination search, voice guidance, guidance display and a wireless remote control.
The system's hard drive is contained in a small box that fits in the car's trunk.

Navigational maps are stored on compact discs, which are available for eight U.S. regions -- California/Nevada, Midwest, Northeast, Mid-Atlantic and Southeast and Texas. Alpine said it will distribute additional and updated CD-ROMs directly to customers.

For more information about the NVA-N751A Voice Guidance Navigation System, contact the company at Alpine Electronics, 19145 Gramercy Place, Torrance, Calif. 90501. Or call 310-783-7004. Alpine's web address is http://www.alpine1.com.
Healthy Choice, the line of nutritionally oriented food, has introduced Mediterranean Harvest, a new line of pasta sauces based on Mediterranean styles.
The sauces come in three flavors: roasted garlic and romano, marinara with burgundy wine, and sun-dried tomato and herb.
The sauces sell for $1.79 to $1.99 for a 26-ounce jar.
The sauces will be available soon. A high-value coupon good for the new sauces will appear beginning in September.
A new book has been published that attempts to teach parents what their kids are able to pick up in two seconds -- how to navigate the Internet.
The goal of "GoodParents.com: What every good parent should know about the Internet" is to keep kids on the path to educational and entertaining use of the Internet.

Written by Robert Maynard, an Internet expert and father of two, it offers simple tips that parents can using immediately to shepherd their kids into the networked world of the future even if the parents have no need to use a computer at all.

"I wrote this book to give even the most computer-phobic parent enough skills to get their kids started in the right direction, keep an eye on what they are doing, and help keep them safe without having to become an expert on the computer or the Internet," Maynard said.

The book, which comes with a CD-ROM, is available from the publisher, The Fidelis Group, at 800/GOODPARENTS (800-466-3727). It costs $19.95. It can also be ordered online through the Web site http://www.goodparents.com.
